summary: Describes how to take a URI and find an authoritative server for information about it, using the Dynamic Delegation Discovery System. It is part four of the DDDS series and replaces RFCs 2168 and 2915.

plainLanguage.summary: This DDDS application uses DNS records to find a server that can provide information about a URI or URN. It follows lookup rules from the name's scheme or namespace until it reaches a server or another defined result.

questions: how to find the authoritative server for a uri
how does ddds resolve a uri
what are the ddds s a u p flags
subtitle: How DDDS uses DNS rules to locate a server with information about a URI or URN.

tldr.problem: A URI or URN may not identify the server that can provide information about the resource, so a client needs a way to locate an authority.
tldr.mechanism: The application uses the URI scheme or URN namespace as an initial key, retrieves NAPTR records from DNS, and follows rewrite rules until a terminal flag indicates the next action.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3404 defines URI and URN resolution applications and a DNS-based database profile. It obsoletes RFC 2168 and RFC 2915 but leaves communication with the resolver to other specifications.

today: RFC 3404 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2002 and obsoletes RFC 2168 and RFC 2915. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Locating a URI Authority
sections.content:
RFC 3404 defines a Dynamic Delegation Discovery System (DDDS) application for locating an authoritative server with information about a URI. It also defines a technically similar application for URNs.

The document defines the application rules, not the general DDDS algorithm or the DNS database format. Those are specified in other parts of the DDDS series, which the RFC says must be read together.

DNS is used to locate resolvers, not to store all information about each resource. The lookup rules turn a URI or URN into keys that lead to a resolver.
sections.plainLanguage: A URI identifies a resource but may not identify the server that has information about it. This application uses DNS to find that server.

sections.title: Separate URI and URN Applications
sections.content:
The RFC defines separate URI and URN applications so that URN resolution can proceed even if generic URI resolution is not widely used. Their rules are technically identical, but they begin from different information.

Generic URI resolution starts with rules for a URI scheme in uri.arpa.. A rule for the urn scheme can direct the process to urn.arpa., where records are organized by URN namespace identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: URI and URN resolution use separate starting points. This lets URN lookups continue without depending on generic URI resolution.

sections.title: The Input and First Lookup Key
sections.content:
The Application Unique String is the URI or URN whose authoritative server is being located. The input MUST be canonicalized and hex encoded as specified by the URI syntax referenced in the RFC.

For a URI, the First Well-Known Rule takes the scheme as the first key. For a URN, it takes the namespace identifier. For example, the URI http://www.example.com/ starts with key http, while urn:foo:foospace starts with foo.
sections.plainLanguage: The first lookup key comes from the start of the name. It is the URI scheme for a URI or the namespace identifier for a URN.

sections.title: Flags and Service Descriptions
sections.content:
Each rule has a flags field and a services field. The terminal flags S, A, and U stop the DDDS loop and specify an SRV lookup, an address lookup, or a URI result. The P flag hands the remaining work to application-specific rules.

Flags are mutually exclusive in this specification. A client MUST ignore a record with an unknown flag and try the next rule; it MUST NOT assume the field contains only one character.

The services field names a protocol and zero or more resolution services. The protocol and each service may be up to 32 characters and must begin with a letter. A protocol identifier needs a URI-resolution-specific specification.
sections.plainLanguage: A rule's flag says whether the DDDS lookup ends or hands work to another procedure. Its service field describes the protocol and service the result supports.

sections.title: NAPTR Records in DNS
sections.content:
The RFC specifies the DNS database defined in RFC 3403, which stores rewrite rules in NAPTR resource records. The URI scheme followed by .uri.arpa. forms the first DNS key; a URN namespace followed by .urn.arpa. forms its key.

NAPTR records return new keys, also represented as domain names. DNS servers MAY include related SRV and address records in the Additional Information section; clients are encouraged, but not required, to use them.

If a record at a given order matches but the client does not support its service, it SHOULD try other records with that same order. It MUST NOT continue to records with a higher order value.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS stores the rewrite rules as NAPTR records. Each answer gives the client a next key or tells it which final lookup to make.

sections.title: Example Lookup Paths
sections.content:
In the RFC's hypothetical URN example, the namespace foo produces the key foo.urn.arpa.. NAPTR records offer services; a client that supports RCDS can then look up SRV records for the service host and receive host and port information.

The HTTP example starts with http, then applies a rule to extract www.example.com. Another lookup can return mirror-service names, which lead to SRV records for the hosts.

The CID example is explicitly illustrative and does not conform to the actual CID URI scheme.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show DNS returning a new key at each step. A terminal result can identify a service name that the client resolves to a host.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The uri.arpa. and urn.arpa. registries are subject to denial-of-service and DNS spoofing attacks. The RFC notes that DNSSEC interactions were still under study when it was written.

Rewrite rules also expose identifiers to risks similar to those of domain names. Implementations should check regular expressions rather than pass them blindly to a general-purpose interpreter. Communication with the resolver is outside this RFC's scope.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS records can be spoofed, and a false rule can send a lookup to the wrong place. Resolver communication needs security rules defined by the protocol that uses it.
